tldr: This paper presents a continual learning framework for humanoid robots that lets them sequentially learn new whole-body motions without forgetting previously mastered skills. By automatically guiding parameter allocation for LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) and knowledge inheritance based on motion similarity, the method cuts training time by up to 40.8% and trainable parameters by up to 94.5% while achieving strong transfer performance, successfully deploying on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN. Whenever a new motion task arrives, past network columns are frozen to prevent catastrophic forgetting by design. The model inherits weights from the most similar parent task and adds lightweight LoRA adapters scaled to the motion similarity. Finally, the teacher policy is distilled into a single student policy for deployment on the physical humanoid robot.
overview:
Research on humanoid robots mastering diverse whole-body dynamic motions—such as walking, running, dancing, and fighting—has made great strides. However, existing reinforcement learning controllers are typically trained offline all at once and then frozen. If you try to teach the robot a new skill later via fine-tuning, catastrophic forgetting occurs, eroding previously mastered skills.

To address this, the authors built a continual learning pipeline for humanoid whole-body motion that sequentially acquires new skills without revisiting past data. The core idea combines the architectural zero-forgetting guarantee of Progressive Neural Networks (PNN)—which adds a new network column per task and freezes past columns—with parameter-efficient LoRA, widely used in large language models.

In addition, the authors quantify the similarity between new and past motions beforehand using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) combined with Optimal Transport (OT). They designed a mechanism that inherits weights from the most similar past task (parent column inheritance) and adaptively assigns a smaller LoRA rank to highly similar tasks and a larger rank to distinct tasks.

Across experiments on six sequentially learned skill categories (walk, run, jump, dance, fight, fall_and_up), the method completely prevented catastrophic forgetting while achieving a forward transfer score of 0.125, significantly outperforming existing baselines (0.079). It also saved up to 94.5% of trainable parameters and up to 40.8% of training time. Finally, the learned controller achieved a 96.13% sim-to-sim transfer rate from Isaac Gym to MuJoCo and a 90.33% success rate on the physical Unitree G1 humanoid, validating its ability to execute sequential skills in the real world.
contributions: Formulated the first continual learning framework and benchmark for humanoid whole-body motion, sequentially adding skills without catastrophic forgetting.
Proposed a two-level motion-similarity measure combining DTW and Optimal Transport (OT) to automate parent task selection and adaptive LoRA rank allocation.
Combined PNN's zero-forgetting-by-construction guarantee with LoRA's parameter efficiency, saving up to 94.5% of trainable parameters and 40.8% of training time.
Demonstrated the execution of 30 distinct motions across 6 categories on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid via distillation from a privileged continual teacher into a single student policy.

sections.heading: Why do humanoids need continual learning?
sections.summary: Whole-body controllers are typically trained offline and frozen, causing catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuned on new skills. To resolve this stability-plasticity dilemma, the paper introduces a continual learning framework combining PNN's zero-forgetting architecture with similarity-guided LoRA.
sections.details:
Humanoid whole-body control is a challenging task that requires coordinating the legs, torso, and arms to maintain balance and momentum while executing dynamic tasks. Recently, reinforcement learning leveraging large-scale human motion data has enabled single controllers to track agile motions.

However, existing controllers are fundamentally designed to be trained offline and then frozen. If you try to teach such a controller a new skill via fine-tuning, catastrophic forgetting erodes already mastered skills. This stands in stark contrast to human learning, where we continually acquire new skills while preserving past proficiencies.

Continual learning aims to solve this dilemma. Yet, prior continual learning in robotics has focused mainly on manipulation or wheeled navigation; it had not been systematically studied for high-DOF bipedal humanoid whole-body motion.

The authors focused on Progressive Neural Networks (PNN), which structurally eliminate forgetting by freezing network columns dedicated to past tasks. However, standard PNNs expand significantly with each new task and learn from scratch, leading to high training costs. This paper overcomes these drawbacks with Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN, which measures motion similarity to inherit weights from the closest past skill and trains only lightweight LoRA parameters.

sections.heading: At the intersection of whole-body locomotion and continual learning
sections.summary: The authors review advances in motion-tracking humanoid control and continual learning techniques for mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Because continual robotics had focused on manipulation, applying it to humanoid whole-body locomotion was unexplored territory.
sections.details:
### Humanoid Whole-Body Locomotion
Reinforcement learning for humanoid control has advanced rapidly in recent years. Robust locomotion using proprioceptive history, coordinated upper- and lower-body control, and generalist controllers tracking thousands of motion clips have emerged. However, all these models are deployed as static policies; expanding their repertoire requires training from scratch.

### Continual Learning
In continual learning, balancing the stability-plasticity dilemma across non-stationary task streams has long been studied. The primary approaches fall into three categories:
- Regularization-based methods that penalize changes to important weights (e.g., EWC)
- Parameter-isolation methods that mask or isolate weights per task (e.g., PackNet)
- Architecture-expansion methods that dynamically grow the network (e.g., PNN)

Recently, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA have also been applied to foundation models to prevent interference. In robotics, continual learning has been explored in mobile manipulation and language-conditioned skill composition, but whole-body humanoid motion control remained unaddressed. This paper fills that gap.

sections.heading: Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN: Lightweight, similarity-driven expansion
sections.summary: By freezing past columns in a PNN, forgetting is eliminated by construction, while motion similarity between tasks is quantified via DTW and Optimal Transport. Initializing weights from the closest parent and adjusting LoRA rank according to similarity yields highly efficient, accurate learning.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The robot sequentially learns a task stream $\{\mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K\}$ one task at a time, without revisiting past data. Because catastrophic forgetting is prevented by construction, the central questions become how quickly knowledge transfers forward and how efficiently parameter growth scales.

### 3.2 Continual Policy Backbone (PNN)
Each task is formulated as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning in joint space using PPO. When learning task $k$, a new MLP column is instantiated and receives lateral connections from all past columns ($1 \dots k-1$). Because prior columns are completely frozen, forgetting due to interference cannot happen by design.

### 3.3 Parameter-Efficient Adaptation (LoRA and Similarity Guidance)
Naively training a full PNN column per task incurs significant computational overhead. The authors address this in two steps:
- **Parent Column Inheritance**: Using precomputed motion similarity $S(l, k)$, the weights of the most similar past task $p(k)$ are copied as a warm-start initialization.
- **Similarity-Guided LoRA Rank Selection**: Linear layer weight updates use low-rank factorization $W + W_B W_A$. Furthermore, the authors introduce an inverse-scaling rule: highly similar motions need only a small rank ($r=4$), while novel motions receive a larger rank ($r=16$).

### 3.4 Motion Similarity via DTW and Optimal Transport
To evaluate similarity between tasks, the authors design a two-level hierarchical distance using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for local time-window alignment and Optimal Transport (OT) for comparing sets of windows across entire motions. Per-frame features include translation- and heading-invariant local velocity, yaw rate, and joint rotation changes. The precomputed distance matrix (Fig. F3) reveals that running is an outlier distinct from all other tasks, whereas walking shares strong stepping coordination with dance and fall-and-up motions.

### 3.5 Teacher-Student Distillation
The teacher policy trained in Isaac Gym with privileged information (base linear velocity, contact states, etc.) is distilled into a single student policy via DAgger, taking only history of onboard proprioceptive states as input.

captions.F3: Motion distance matrix across the six skill categories (lighter colors indicate higher similarity). Walking is close to other skills and acts as a frequent knowledge source, whereas running is distant and largely distinct from the rest.

sections.heading: Zero forgetting, efficient forward transfer, and physical G1 deployment
sections.summary: Evaluations across six whole-body motion tasks show that the proposed method maintains near-zero forgetting while achieving the highest forward transfer (0.125). It cuts parameters by 94.5% and training time by 40.8%, reaching a 90.33% success rate on the physical Unitree G1.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used six motion tasks from the LAFAN1 and Kungfu datasets, learned in sequence: walk $\rightarrow$ run $\rightarrow$ jump $\rightarrow$ dance $\rightarrow$ fight $\rightarrow$ fall_and_up. Baselines included state-of-the-art humanoid imitation models adapted to continual learning (KungfuBot2, ASAP, HumanoidVerse) and standard continual learning algorithms (EWC, PackNet). Metrics include Average Accuracy (AA), Forgetting Measure (FM), Backward Transfer (BWT), and Forward Transfer (FWT).

### 4.2 Main Results
The proposed method (sim-LoRA) achieves $\text{FM} \approx 0$ by construction. Notably, it attains an FWT of $0.125$, well above the strongest baseline KungfuBot2 ($0.079$). Its Average Accuracy (AA) reached $0.945$, leading all approaches. EWC and PackNet, unable to exploit motion structure for transfer, scored low AA values of $0.488$ and $0.586$, respectively.

### 4.3 Ablations and Efficiency
Removing PNN and using a single backbone caused noticeable forgetting (FM jumped from $0.000$ to $0.137$), confirming that column isolation is essential. In addition, LoRA rank allocation showed steady accuracy gains when moving from fixed ($0.895$) to binned ($0.928$) and linear similarity-guided scaling ($0.945$).
Compared to full fine-tuning of PNN columns, LoRA reduced trainable parameters by up to $94.5\%$ (2.4M $\rightarrow$ 132K) and wall-clock training time per 5k iterations by up to $40.8\%$ (2.94h $\rightarrow$ 1.74h).

### 4.4 Sim-to-Sim Transfer and Real-Robot Deployment
In sim-to-sim transfer from Isaac Gym to MuJoCo, the controller achieved a $96.13\%$ success rate. Deployed onto the physical 23-DOF Unitree G1 humanoid, the single distilled student policy was tested across 30 distinct motions spanning all 6 categories, achieving an overall real-world success rate of $90.33\%$ (10 trials per motion).

The proposed method (blue line) confines forgetting (FM) and backward degradation (BWT) to near zero, while expanding outward on Average Accuracy (AA) and Forward Transfer (FWT).
captions.F6: Qualitative comparison of the distilled student policy in Isaac Gym (left) versus MuJoCo (right). Across dance, fall_and_up, fight, and run skills, motion tracking remains consistent across physics simulators.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: Combining PNN's zero-forgetting architecture with similarity-guided adaptive LoRA establishes an efficient, accurate continual learning system for humanoid whole-body motions. Its successful real-robot deployment points the way toward an ever-evolving generalist controller.
sections.details:
This paper proposed a continual learning framework allowing humanoid robots to sequentially acquire diverse whole-body skills without catastrophic forgetting.

Grounding the architecture in PNN ensures zero forgetting by design. Guiding parent inheritance and LoRA rank allocation through DTW and Optimal Transport motion similarity delivered dramatic parameter and computation savings (up to 94.5% fewer parameters, 40.8% less training time) alongside superior forward transfer.

Finally, distilling the continual teacher into a single student policy enabled stable execution of diverse motions—from walking to martial arts—on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid. This demonstrates a practical foundational technology for scalable humanoid control that removes the need to retrain controllers from scratch whenever a new skill is taught.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details for motion similarity and training
sections.summary: Details on the motion data format, DTW and Optimal Transport (Sinkhorn) parameters, and reward and domain randomization configurations for PPO reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
### Motion Data Format and Features
Retargeted motion clips are resampled to 30 Hz and contain root translation, quaternion rotation, joint axis-angle representations, and contact masks (allowing soft labels). Translation- and heading-invariant feature vectors are computed using local linear velocity, yaw rate, and geodesic changes in joint angles.

### Optimal Transport and DTW Computation
Scale robustness is achieved by averaging across four window length and stride configurations: $(3, 2), (5, 3), (10, 7), (15, 10)$ seconds. Sakoe-Chiba band constraints are applied to window-level DTW, and the cross-window/cross-motion Optimal Transport problem is solved efficiently via Sinkhorn iterations. Because similarity is computed offline once, it incurs no reinforcement learning runtime overhead.

### Reward Design and Domain Randomization
The PPO reward consists of exponential tracking terms for root velocity and key-body positions, orientations, and velocities, along with regularization penalties on action rate, joint acceleration, foot slip, and self-collision. For sim-to-real transfer, domain randomization is applied across link mass, friction coefficient, PD gains, and motor strength.

takeaways: Rather than relying on regularization to curb forgetting, structurally guaranteeing zero forgetting with PNN and minimizing expansion costs with LoRA proves remarkably effective and practical for robotics.

Pre-quantifying motion similarity using DTW and Optimal Transport (OT) intelligently informs warm-start sources and LoRA capacity, driving substantial gains in training efficiency and forward transfer.

Distilling a continually learned teacher into a single student policy via DAgger eliminates architectural complexity at deployment time, maintaining high success rates on physical humanoids like the Unitree G1.
limitations: As tasks increase, PNN lateral connections scale as $O(K^2)$. Scaling to dozens or hundreds of tasks in the long term may require additional pruning or routing mechanisms.
The method assumes a task-incremental setting where task boundaries are clearly defined; extending to task-free or class-incremental setups without task identifiers remains future work.
Computing motion similarity requires retargeted reference motion data to be available prior to training.
